newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: World's most valuable stamp to be sold.
newsitem.headline: World's most valuable stamp to be sold.

text.p: The world's most valuable single postage stamp, rescued by a Swedish schoolboy in 1885 from his grandmother's rubbish bin, will be put on sale in Zurich next month, the auction house said on Wednesday.

The so-called "Treskilling Yellow", issued in Sweden in 1857 but for many years suspected to be a fake, has an estimated price of up to $1.2 million but could bring much more, according to experts on the world's booming philately market.

"This is the unique stamp that all great collectors have been talking about for over 100 years," David Feldman, Irish director of his own Geneva-based auctioneers company told Reuters. "And some of the greatest have owned it."

The flimsy, orange-yellow stamp is already hailed in the Guinness Book of World Records as the most valuable object of any type by weight, volume and density since it was last sold for just over $1.2 million in 1990.

It is being sold again on November 8 because the 1990 buyer, a Swedish enthusiast, never fully paid for it and has offered it up to cover his remaining debt and other charges, according to the auction house.
The "Treskilling", or three-shilling, was the first stamp issued by Sweden in 1855, 15 years after Britain issued the first postage stamps in 1840.
But it was printed in green -- and the yellow specimen found by schoolboy Georg Backman on an envelope during a summer holiday at his grandmother's house is the only one ever to have surfaced.

Backman sold it to a Stockholm dealer for just seven Swedish kronor, just a few dollars at the time. But by 1894 its rarity had brought it to the attention of German-French collector Philippe la Renotiere von Ferray.
La Renotiere, regarded by historians of philately as one of the greatest collectors of all time, bequeathed it with his entire collection to the Berlin Museum on his death in 1918.
However, the collection was seized by French authorities as part of reparation claims against Germany following World War One and soon was back on the international market.
In 1937 the "Treskilling" was sold to then King Carol of Romania and after World War Two it passed through several collections.

In the 1970s, some Swedish experts -- puzzled that no other yellow versions of what should have been a green stamp had been found -- suggested it was a forgery. But a scientific examination using laser technology established it was genuine.

Feldman, who in 1993 sold the so-called "crown jewel of philately" -- two fabled stamps from the British colony of Mauritius on their original envelope -- for $3.8 million, first auctioned the "Treskilling" in 1984.
Offered by a Swiss bank, it fetched just under $500,000 from a Swedish collector whose son put it back on the market through the Irish auctioneer in 1990.
Feldman, whose company has handled the auction of many of the world's best-known philatelic items, said interest at the 1984 and 1990 sales of the "Treskilling" was the highest he had ever known.

"I have never seen so many bidding hands in a stamp auction room, and I think the spectacle will be similar next month," he said. "After all, the new owner not only becomes part of the legend but achieves philatelic immortality by buying it."
